questions.title: Repeatedly practising under the influence of alcohol
questions.question: A doctor repeatedly treating his patient under the influence of alcohol is doing:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Civil negligence is a careless breach of the duty of care that harms a specific patient; repeatedly practising while intoxicated is judged as a disciplinary breach of professional standards rather than as a single negligent clinical act.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dichotomy (fee-splitting) is the unethical sharing of fees in return for patient referral; it has nothing to do with practising under the influence of alcohol.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Privileged communication refers to legally protected confidential information between doctor and patient; it is not a form of wrongdoing at all.
explanations.D: Correct. Repeatedly treating patients while under the influence of alcohol is professional misconduct — infamous conduct in a professional respect that falls below the standards expected of the profession. It reflects a pattern of unfitness to practise safely and is handled by the medical syndicate's disciplinary process rather than as a single act of civil negligence. Practising while impaired endangers every patient seen and breaches the doctor's ethical duty to be fit for duty.

questions.learning_objective: Classify repeatedly practising under the influence of alcohol as professional misconduct.

questions.title: Ground for erasing a physician's registration
questions.question: A physician's registration may be erased from the medical syndicate if he:

options.B: Is involved in a private job.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Owning more than one clinic is permitted and is not a ground for erasing a physician's name from the register.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Holding a private job alongside practice is not, by itself, a disciplinary ground for erasure from the syndicate register.
explanations.C: Correct. A physician's name may be erased (struck off) from the medical syndicate register when he is convicted of a criminal offence, because a criminal conviction demonstrates unfitness to remain on the professional register. Erasure is a disciplinary sanction reserved for serious wrongdoing such as crime or grave professional misconduct, not for ordinary administrative facts. It removes the legal right to practise.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reaching pension age ends active service but does not erase the doctor's name from the register as a disciplinary measure.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a criminal conviction as a ground for erasing a doctor from the medical syndicate register.

field_notes.sourceDuplicates: Q95/Q98 repeat this erasure item (held); Q110 T/F excluded

questions.title: Physical harassment of a patient during examination
questions.question: During examination, a female patient experienced verbal and physical harassment by the physician. She filed a complaint against him. The physician can be sued for which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Verbal and, especially, physical harassment of a patient during examination is an assault — an intentional act that threatens or inflicts unlawful physical contact, for which the physician can be sued in the courts. Assault is a criminal and civil wrong distinct from clinical error, because it is a deliberate violation of the patient's person rather than a lapse of care. The patient's complaint therefore founds a legal action for assault.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Incompetence is a lack of reasonable skill or knowledge in providing care; harassment is a deliberate wrongful act, not a deficiency of clinical ability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Negligence is a careless failure to meet the standard of care; harassment is intentional misconduct, not carelessness, so it is not negligence.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Although harassment is also unprofessional, the specific ground on which the physician can be sued in court is assault; professional misconduct is dealt with by the syndicate's disciplinary process rather than by a lawsuit.

questions.learning_objective: Identify physical harassment of a patient as an assault for which the physician can be sued.

questions.title: Advertising one's expertise in newspapers
questions.question: A doctor repeatedly advertising about his professional expertise in a newspaper is doing a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Privileged communication is protected confidential doctor-patient information; it is unrelated to advertising.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Civil negligence is a careless breach of the duty of care that harms a patient; self-advertising harms no individual patient and is instead an ethical breach.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dichotomy is fee-splitting for referrals; it is a different offence from advertising one's expertise.
explanations.D: Correct. A doctor who repeatedly advertises his professional expertise in newspapers is committing professional misconduct, because self-promotion and soliciting patients through advertising breach the profession's ethical rules on dignified, non-commercial practice. Such conduct is judged by the medical syndicate as infamous conduct in a professional respect. It is an offence against professional standards rather than a civil wrong against a particular patient.

questions.learning_objective: Classify self-advertising of professional expertise as professional misconduct.

field_notes.sourceDuplicates: Q94 repeats this advertising item with reordered options (held)

questions.title: Senior surgeon persisting with outdated operative technique
questions.question: Dr. X is alarmed by the behavior of the senior surgeon in the operating room. The surgeon uses out-of-date techniques that prolong operations and result in greater post-operative pain and longer recovery time. This case is an example of:

explanations.A: Correct. A surgeon who uses out-of-date techniques that prolong operations and cause greater pain and slower recovery is committing medical malpractice — substandard professional treatment that harms patients. Malpractice is the umbrella term for care that falls below the accepted standard and injures the patient, which is exactly what outdated, harmful operative technique does. The demonstrable harm (added pain, longer recovery) is the injury that makes it malpractice rather than a mere ethical lapse.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Professional misconduct covers ethical or disciplinary offences (advertising, impairment, dishonesty); using outmoded surgical technique is a failure of clinical standard that harms patients, i.e. malpractice, not an ethics offence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Negligence can be one element underlying malpractice, but the best single description of substandard technique that injures patients is medical malpractice; here the pattern of harmful practice is the malpractice itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Incompetence is a lack of skill or knowledge; a senior surgeon who is capable but persists with outdated methods is delivering substandard care (malpractice) rather than simply lacking ability.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise harm from persistently outdated operative technique as medical malpractice.

field_notes.conceptReuse: reuses CON-MUL-C88F76100B04D9 (outdated-technique harm) from the medical-errors/malpractice tranche

questions.title: Crude jokes about patients that disturb colleagues
questions.question: Dr. X is accustomed to make frequent crude jokes about the patients that obviously bother the assisting nurses. This attitude is considered:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Incompetence is a lack of skill or knowledge; making crude jokes reflects unprofessional behaviour, not a deficiency of clinical ability.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Medical malpractice is substandard treatment that harms a patient; distasteful jokes do not constitute negligent or harmful treatment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Negligence is a careless failure in the standard of care causing harm; offensive jokes are an attitude and behaviour problem, not a lapse in clinical care.
explanations.D: Correct. A doctor who habitually makes crude jokes about patients that disturb colleagues is displaying professional misconduct — conduct that is unbecoming and disrespectful and falls below the ethical standards of the profession. Professionalism requires respect and courtesy toward patients and the healthcare team, and persistently disrespectful conduct breaches that duty. It is a disciplinary and ethical matter judged as misconduct rather than a clinical error.

questions.learning_objective: Classify persistently disrespectful behaviour toward patients as professional misconduct.

questions.title: Appellate body for a professional-misconduct decision
questions.question: Appeal against the professional misconduct is made to:

explanations.A: Correct. An appeal against a finding of professional misconduct is made to the Egyptian Medical Syndicate, which holds disciplinary jurisdiction over its members. Because professional misconduct is judged within the profession's own disciplinary structure, the appeal is heard by the syndicate rather than by the general courts or the ministry. The syndicate's disciplinary bodies both impose and review sanctions against doctors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Ministry of Health administers health services but is not the appellate body for a professional-misconduct decision, which lies with the syndicate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ordinary court handles criminal and civil suits, not the internal disciplinary appeal against a professional-misconduct finding.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since the correct route is specifically the syndicate, 'all of the above' is wrong; the ministry and the court are not the appellate authorities here.

questions.learning_objective: State that an appeal against a professional-misconduct decision is made to the Egyptian Medical Syndicate.

field_notes.corroboration: Q111 T/F confirms appeal is to the Medical Syndicate (key True)

questions.title: What professional misconduct includes
questions.question: Professional misconduct includes:

options.A: Immoral conduct in the practice of the profession.
options.B: Permitting or aiding an unlicensed person to perform activities without a license.
options.C: Refusing a client or patient's service because of greed, color or national origin.

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Immoral conduct in practice is indeed professional misconduct, but it is only one of the listed examples, so it cannot be the complete answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own. Permitting or aiding an unlicensed person to practise is professional misconduct, but it is not the only correct example listed.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. Refusing a patient's service out of greed or discrimination (colour, national origin) is professional misconduct, yet it too is only one instance among the options.
explanations.D: Correct. Professional misconduct is a broad category that includes all of these: immoral conduct in the practice of the profession, permitting or aiding an unlicensed person to perform medical activities, and refusing a patient's service out of greed or discrimination. Because each listed behaviour is a recognised form of infamous professional conduct, 'all of the above' is the complete answer. The heading of misconduct groups these diverse ethical breaches together.

questions.learning_objective: List immoral conduct, aiding unlicensed practice, and discriminatory refusal of care as forms of professional misconduct.

questions.title: Sequence of disciplinary actions for disgraceful behaviour
questions.question: The disciplinary actions of the medical council in case of disgraceful behavior of a doctor are taken in the following sequence:

explanations.A: Correct. The disciplinary actions of the medical council for a doctor's disgraceful behaviour escalate in the sequence alarm, warning, blame, then temporary revocation of the licence. The order runs from the mildest measure (an alarm or caution) through warning and blame to the most severe short of permanent erasure (temporary suspension). This graduated ladder matches the sanction to the seriousness and repetition of the conduct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Temporary revocation is the most severe step and cannot come first; the sanctions begin with the mildest measure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Blame is not the first action; the ladder opens with an alarm or caution before blame.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The correct opening step is the alarm, not a warning; this option also misorders the early sanctions.

questions.learning_objective: Order the medical council's disciplinary actions: alarm, warning, blame, then temporary revocation.

field_notes.corroboration: Q109 T/F confirms temporary revocation is NOT the first action (key False)
